utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher lift the blinds, please, because I'm about to issue a ruling. Kindly call the case, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today we are Thursday. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people assisting us. I shall hand down an oral decision, and I shall read it out slowly. It's a lengthy ruling. Oral decision asking the Defence to notify the Prosecution of its intention of invoking a defence of alibi or any special defence. At this stage of the trial, the Trial Chamber feels it is necessary to ask the Defence teams to notify the Prosecution of their intent to invoke, if need be, a defence of alibi or any special defence. The Trial Chamber recalls that on the 13th of September, 2007, it had asked the parties to submit its arguments on the question as to at what point in time of the trial the Defence teams would notify the Prosecution of their intent to invoke, if need be, a defence of alibi or any special defence pursuant to Rule 67 of the Rules. In its written submission filed on the 19th of September, 2007, Defence counsel of the accused Praljak, supported by Defence counsel of the accused Coric, ascertained that such a notification could take place at any point in time during the trial and at the earliest at the end of the Prosecution's case. Other Defence counsel did not react. In its submission filed on the 24th of September, 2007, the Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to set a time for the notification in the near future pursuant to Rule 67 of the Rules. Pursuant to Rule 67(A) of the Rules, the Trial Chamber does have a discretionary power and is entitled to set a notification deadline. The Trial Chamber holds that by virtue of this power it should make sure that the trial is expeditious and fair. It holds that pursuant to Rule 67(A)(ii) of the Rules, in lower case, that the notification should take place before the end of the Prosecution case so as to enable the Prosecution to challenge any special defence or defence of alibi. Therefore, pursuant to Rule 67 of the Rules, the Trial Chamber is asking the Defence teams to let the Prosecution know of their intent to invoke or not a defence of alibi or any special defence before the 17th of October 2007. Briefly, the Trial Chamber holds - I'm sure you have understood this - that as far as the Bench is concerned, the Defence teams should let the Prosecution team know before the end of the Prosecution case if the Defence teams have any intention of invoking any defence of alibi or any special defence so as to enable, if the Defence so wishes, to enable the Prosecution to prepare for this. So you will have until the 17th of October, 2007, to let the Prosecution know whether or not you wish to invoke a defence of alibi or any special defence. This was a lengthy ruling, but it was important at this juncture of the trial. We shall now drop the blinds. As far as our calculations are concerned, Mr. Praljak, yesterday you had, as I had already said, 80 minutes. You have had other accused's time. Some of the accused have not taken the floor and should have 30 minutes each, that is Defence Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. We said on the first day that we have no questions, that is to say Mr. Coric's Defence has no questions for this witness, just to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring in the witness. Let me take this opportunity to say this to Mr. Praljak: Yesterday, we didn't quite understand what you were getting at and what the meaning of your questions was, so one could have the feeling that we are wasting our time. Please be accurate that we understand what it is you want from the witness so that we understand what your defence case is about, because if we don't understand what you're getting at, we're wasting our time. So if you see that the Judges are querulous about it, please be as accurate as you can. Otherwise we feel that we are wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you know why you are putting the question to the witness. You have a number of documents. You know which witnesses you will call to come and testify. We don't have those documents. So notwithstanding the knowledge the Judges may have of this case, sometimes we are going about it blindly, and when you are putting questions on information which we don't have, then we are lost. This is what I wanted to share with you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning to Your Honours. Thank you for issuing that caution. I'm sure that certain questions have remained unclear, although I didn't feel so myself, but I did want to clarify certain matters, especially with respect to what the witness knows first-hand in relation to certain documents, because I understood it that the statement given in the first person or the reports in the first person means that he had available to him all the information. However, I will be more specific today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Anyway, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like -- I would like to greet the witness. And the representative of the Spanish government. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to ask from my binder of documents which you all have to take a look at 3D 01089. 3D 01089. It's the 19th, 1993, signed by Major General Milivoj Petkovic in Kiseljak, the 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We have the document on our screens, so please take a look at the document, Witness, in which it says that the date is the 19th of October, and it is in Kiseljak, and the readiness to implement the joint declaration that was signed by the President Franjo Tudjman and the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and that it is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I can not find that document. Can you give me the number again or help me find it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 01089. This is what it looks like. It's in the binder with the green stickers, green tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I help in this matter. Mr. Praljak, we have two documents which you submitted. The one which was submitted on the 7th of -- I'm sorry. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have prepared a set of documents -- well, I prepared one for the first witness and for the second witness, but as some of the topics are the same --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But anyway, Witness, have you found the document, 3D 01089?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI

utterances.text: It says there that in taking over the obligation at talks with General Briquemont in Kiseljak on behalf of the Main Staff of the HVO, Mr. Petkovic gave his agreement under 1 that the engineer's units of UNPROFOR can start with preparations and building the bridge at Bijela; 2, that the HVO would refrain from any military action; and that the Main Staff will give permission for the all-round presence of military observers at HVO headquarters north throughout the construction of the bridge. utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is the first time I see this document, first time I see this document. The document is not intended to the Madrid Task Force.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's like this, sir: My question is a very simple one. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question wasn't whether you have seen the document and who it was addressed to. My question is were you in any way acquainted with the contents of the document? Because after that you went to see how things stood. So did you know of the contents of this document, what the document says, when you were there? It's a very simple technical question, so please give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General. I must say that I do not know this document, but the fact is that on the 16th of October, the first reconnaissance mission was conducted on the Bijela Bridge in order to start the technical studies. So this of course had the result that UNPROFOR was able to get to the Bijela Bridge in order to conduct that reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask for two things. First of all, to have document 4D 00711 up on e-court, and it is a document in Mr. Petkovic's binder, towards the end. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for getting up, but I see that the binders that the Petkovic Defence intended for the Judges and the witness still haven't been distributed, so would the usher hand those documents over to you, to the Trial Chamber, and to the witness. But we did see it to the Prosecution, so they already have the set of documents. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, would you place the map on the ELMO while we look for 4D 00711, while that appears. Witness, take a look at the map on the ELMO. It's a military map. As I said, it's a military map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If the usher would be so kind as to put the map on the ELMO. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in so we can see the four circles. It's the northern part of -- no, zoom out. Zoom out so we can see all four circles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's called the contra-zoom. So look at the map, please, and under point 1 we have Vrdi, and then Mali Vrdi. Can you see that, Vrdi? Is that the position at Vrdi? Number 2 shows Bijela Bridge. Can you see the bridge there? Number 2, Bijela Bridge. And part of the lake moving to the north.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And number 3 we have the Salakovac dam. Can you see Salakovac dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And number 4 is the Mostar hydroelectric power plant; is that right? I made a mistake and wrote the wrong word there. Now look at 4D 00 -- you know that Mostar was there. That was the hydroelectric power plant, Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, you must give me an audible answer. Thank you. Now look at 4D 00711?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the folder the usher is keeping in hand, the last one is in. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm told that your affirmative answer wasn't recorded, that number 4 is the Mostar hydroelectric power plant. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that speakers make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. In the document that you're going to see now dated the 25th of September, 1993, and at the time you were already there, the document was signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army, and in that document --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have the reference of the document again? I have just been given the binder, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 711. It's the last document in that binder that the usher just gave you. In that document the commander of the 4th Corps, in his order of the 25th of September, 1993, separated the areas of responsibility, divided them up. There was the center area of responsibility, center, then south 2, the third area of responsibility was south 1, and north 1 was the fourth area of responsibility. Now, I'm interested in north 1, the fourth area of responsibility. So can we zoom out so we can see the whole of the map with all four points, and it says to the north of the Ledenice facility is the Bijela creek. And south of north 1 are residential buildings exclusively, north of the Mostar hydroelectric power plant. So that's marked here. Can you see the top-most mauve line where it says Ledenice and this branch of the Bijela river belongs to the north, area of responsibility north, and the hydroelectric power plant area of responsibility. Well anyway we have the north and south border, the delineation of the various areas of responsibility. Based on this order, sir, was Bijela Bridge in the area of responsibility of the BH army of the 4th Corps, 4th Corps of the BH army? Based on this order was the bridge in the area of responsibility of the BH army's 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know so, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, based on this order. I'm not asking you whether you know generally, but based on that order is that what follows based on that order according to your military professional knowledge as a military man reading this order, does clearly state that Belija bridge based on the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have an objection. The witness has been asked. He's answered the question and now what's happening is an argument because he doesn't like the answer he got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I have a question, kind of follow-up question, that you mention now here in your document, in the Defence Mr. Petkovic document, that the zone of responsibility of Operative Group north 1 and A north objective Ledenice-Bijela creek, and now you ask the witness if in view of this order if the bridge was in a way within the framework of the army, I mean the army of Armija. Now, frankly, if I see this Bijela creek, myself, I cannot see how should we take it, because Bijela creek, a smaller river, of course, could be rather long one, and here it doesn't seem to be exactly said which part of the river is being under their control, that is the armija's control, and we do not know where the bridge was in this case. For example, I don't know if Ledenice -- where is Ledenice and where the bridge is being established. So that is why it is rather difficult to answer this, and I'm sure that the witness had the same problem to answer to you, to your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. According to what I have understood, General, the problem runs as follows: We are talking about hydroelectric power plants supply and how the town of Mostar was supplied in electricity. This is an important aspect. If the area where the electricity was produced was under the control of the ABiH, and in at that case you cannot criticise the HVO for having tampered with electrical supply. This I think is the problem as it stands in a general sense. Now, in support the Defence case, it seems to me that General Praljak is showing you a map which we still have in front of us, and on this map we see the Bijela river with the points 1, 2, 3 and 4. This famous bridge is located at point 2. The order which you have in front of you, which is 4D 00711 seems to indicate, seems to indicate - I'm being very cautious here - that this area, so-called Operational Group Sector North group 1, which is explicitly mentioned in the order is under the control of the ABiH. So a simple behind could infer looking at the map and at the document that the electrical power plant is under the control of the ABiH. The general is putting the question to you, and you say, "I don't know." I'm asking you the question at the time you were assuming your duties here. Now, as far as these markings on the map are concerned, was SpaBat patrolling this area, and if it was, the SpaBat must have seen the ABiH at check-points, either the ABiH or the HVO, because it would be inconceivable to have both the HVO and the ABiH in the same area. Why not, of course, but seemingly, according to this order we have in front of us, the ABiH was controlling this area. So this is the question I'm putting to you. What General Praljak is saying, i.e., namely that the ABiH is controlling points 1, 2, 3, and 4 is in line what SpaBat acknowledged, or are you saying you don't know because it happened 14 years ago and it might be very difficult to answer on the spur of the moment such a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to insist on the fact that it was 14 years ago, and also on what my mission was in relevance to the details. Now, let me get back to the question. General Praljak did not ask me in the previous question as to the hydro-electric dam. He asked me about the Bijela Bridge and whether or not it was included in the area of responsibility of the north operational group, and my answer is that I don't know. The demarcation, there's mention of object, and I don't know what that really means. And then there's mention of Bijela creek, and I don't know if that's included or excluded. Now, when a military unit is given an action area, usually specific geographical points are mentioned and it is mentioned whether they are included or excluded. So I don't know here whether the Bijela Bridge is included or excluded. Now, as regards the hydroelectric installation, we see here that with north 1 in the southern part is told that the buildings to the north of the hydroelectric installation and to the dam are excluded. But obviously at the north area of the area of responsibility of the central group these buildings are included, the buildings that are to the north of the dam. That is to say that the dam would not be under the responsibility of group north, but it would be under the responsibility of the central Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A question, (redacted). If we have before us an order which divides the terrain in different operational zones, does that mean that the troops concerned have actual control of that zone, or is it perhaps a wish or a hypothetical, theoretical delineation of -- of areas of interest rather than a reflection of effective control? Could you enlighten us on this? What does it mean an order like this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally the division of the battlefield into areas of responsibility implies that one unit was made responsible for whatever happens in that particular area. It's in charge of defending the area or attacking in the area. Then there are many variations if we talk about where the attack comes from or other technical matters that we can leave aside for the time being. So I understand that these areas are under the control of each one of the sides involved. In military terms, you cannot exclude that from that area through observation or through shelling you could in fact control or observe other areas beyond that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we tried to understand. However -- well, please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, although I'm so confused. It is just amazing how one can complicate the simplest of matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, can you see the Bijela Bridge under number 2 crossing the branch of something that is called the Bijela creek? Please look at it. You can see a bridge going over the Potok-Bijela branch. Do you see that on the map? Could it please be enlarged so that you can nicely see the bridge. Two parallel lines. You can see the circle. Do you see the Bijela bridge? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you see the Bijela bridge as it is drawn here, and there is this creek there, this branch called Potok-Bijela.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see it far better on the map, and I can just about guess where it is from looking at it on the monitor, on the screen. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You see it on the map. We're done with the map then. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I please have a date, a signature on this map, as well as an IC number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to give an IC number. Witness, would you please write "DW" on the map and put the date, today's date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness didn't mark this map. The markings are those of the accused. So I think -- I respectfully suggest that it's sufficient just to give it an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but know we've already had this type of problem and the Trial Chamber decided then that the witness could mark that and then we'll refer back to the transcript to see what the witness said then on the basis of the four circles marked by the person asking the question. So please write in "DW," today's date 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness on the map itself, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do. And we're going to get an IC number, please Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No names. No names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No names, please, just "DW." "DW" and the 5th of October, that's all. No names.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The document just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit number IC 681. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so IC 681. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'd like to ask for two things now. First of all can we look at document 6405, P-0645. It is in the binder containing Prosecution Exhibit. 6405, that is, in the Prosecution binder. So could you please help us with that. The date on this document is the 4th of November. It's a report, a SpaBat report. 6405. P 6405 SpaBat report dated the 4th of November, 1993. The witness was there. I would just like to have a look at paragraph 5 of this document, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, "Other information"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 5 says: "Today a SpaBat patrol confirmed that part of the bridge was destroyed, part of the Bijela bridge that had not been destroyed before. Please find attached a drawing of the bridge before and after this latest destruction." Witness, can you testify as to the report of your unit, which says that on that day -- well, that was the day when it was confirmed that part of the Bijela bridge was destroyed, a part that had not been destroyed before that, and that what was attached there is a sketch of what was the case before and what was the case then. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. In the same binder can you have a look at P 06405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, item 6 I see in this document that new HVO positions were discovered at YH3096. I don't know what this corresponds to. Is that within the AOR of the ABiH or not? But I can see this written at that point. I'm just reminding you by saying so. Please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we now have document 6 E 06 -- oh I have misspoken. Sorry. 65 P 6568. It's in the same binder, the next document. That document is dated the 10th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, although I don't understand why it's 3. This is what it says -- have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before my eyes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, a letter from General Pasalic, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was received at the command of the Spanish Battalion where he informed about the destruction of the remains of the bridge and then he asked whether it was perhaps the Spanish Battalion or the HVO who had blown up the bridge on the 4th of that month as we saw in the previous document. A Spanish Battalion patrol confirmed the two lanes on this bridge had been destroyed that had not been destroyed earlier, that is. My question, Witness, is as follows: According to this report, is it not stated that two lanes of the bridge had not been destroyed and it was established that they were then destroyed on the 4th of November? Just tell me, is that what is written there? That's my first question. Is it written here that two lanes of this bridge were destroyed that had not been destroyed before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document explains the picture we saw in the document that we were shown before. It says that two of the three lanes that were still safe or undamaged were then destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, please. Sir. Sir, please. All right. It's a very simple question. Please, time seems to be running out for me. Just tell me yes or no. Do you confirm what paragraph 3 of the report of the Spanish Battalion says, your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness -- or excuse me, the accused continually suggests that this is the witness's report as though the witness wrote this report. I think that it's clear the witness did not write this report, although it's one that he received and it was written by others. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, sir -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you look at what the Prosecution showed us at first, that is to say those 70 or 80 paragraphs related to this gentleman, the witness, all of them are in the first-person singular. The witness speaks in the first-person singular. Please look at the document. So the Prosecution gave documents of the Spanish Battalion to this witness, and he turned these witnesses into the first-person singular. Now, when I say could this document be confirmed for me, the Spanish Battalion document confirmed, what is being stated is that I'm making an insinuation. I'm just asking for a confirmation. The gentleman can say I don't know anything about this, but that will bring into question the entire report that you the Prosecution submitted on his behalf in the first-person singular, as if the gentleman had been counting shells as if he had been on the APCs, as if he had been where the Italian soldiers got killed, and so on and so forth. So I'm being crystal clear and acting in accordance with the instructions of the Trial Chamber. I'm sticking to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So on the basis of this document of the Spanish Battalion, do you confirm that this is a Spanish Battalion document? For me it is enough if you say that is what my testimony is or that is not what my testimony is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this is a document drawn up by the rapid deployment force which informed in turn SpaBat and which talked about the destruction of the last two lanes that were still standing on the bridge, and I have put my initials to this document, so I have recognised this document as an official document of SpaBat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. This is the way we're supposed to proceed. And another question in relation to this: Since Mr. Pasalic is asking whether you destroyed these two lanes, do you know whether it's the Spanish Battalion that destroyed these two lanes? Was it the Spaniards who did that, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not SpaBat that destroyed or blew up the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course I believe that fully. Now let us look at paragraph 26 of your statement that you gave to the Prosecution. So it is it your statement, paragraph 26 of your statement. This is what it says: "We were involved in security, and we were proffering technical and logistic support in order to re-establish communications between the corridor Mostar-Jablanica-Sarajevo, which was interrupted when the Bijela bridge was destroyed by the HVO. The aim was to ameliorate in this way not only communications but the accomplishment of other missions of the task force as the passage of humanitarian convoys." My question -- actually, I have two questions. To the best of your knowledge, to the best of your knowledge -- or to be more precise, on the basis of what knowledge do you state here explicitly that the HVO destroyed the two remaining lanes of the Bijela bridge? Please tell me and Their Honours and the Prosecutor what your arguments are to claim that it's the HVO that destroyed the remaining two lanes on the Bijela bridge? If you say, "I have no arguments," I will be pleased and we will proceed. And if you say, "I do have arguments," then we can hear you out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no legal proof, or at least no proof of any legal validity to say that the HVO destroyed the bridge. However, our intelligence sources in the field at the time did think that the destruction might be ascribed to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will do. Second question: You say here: If the bridge had been destroyed then, my question is was the bridge used before that? Now, if it was destroyed regardless of whatever Pasalic says, it's the HVO, the Spaniards, in one Spanish Battalion document that I showed the Trial Chamber, it is stated explicitly the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did that. But tell me now, before destruction was this bridge being used? Could people cross that bridge? Not only that bridge but also the other way round. Do you know, do you not no, yes, no, let's move on. I'm asking you to read paragraph 38 of your statement where you say: "After the destruction of the bridge on Bijela, the SpaBat and UNPROFOR continue using the alternative route in the area so as to allow the passage of humanitarian convoys through a mountainous path." That is to say, after the destruction you took alternative routes. Is that what you've stated? So it was used before the destruction and afterwards you started using different roads. Do you stand by what you said in your statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You've put two questions to me. The first one, yes, I did know about that, and I spoke about it yesterday if I'm not mistaken. You recommended to us a bypass around the brook which ends at the Bijela bridge, our sappers or engineers in fact did have a look at that bypass and did not recommend the use of that road for the humanitarian aid convoys. Now, we still went on using the alternative route because the Bijela route was in fact cut off, hence our interest in opening up that particular line or road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will do. It is your testimony that before that the road was usable. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before we see the map could you please look at paragraph 60. Just paragraph 60 of your statement. In paragraph 60 of your statement you say: "In East Mostar the SpaBat prevented or reported the ABiH placing mortars in the proximity of the hospital building while patrolling the area throughout this period." So you say here prevented. That is to say that you succeeded in preventing them from doing that. So in most other cases it -- the wording is different. The SpaBat is trying to prevent, trying to prevent. That is what reports say. To the best of your knowledge, did you have success in preventing the placement of mortars by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the proximity of the hospital, in the proximity of the field hospital that you later put up near the southern camp, and to what extent did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, in this self-same paragraph it is said that we tried to avoid. And as I said yesterday, the patrols that we had in East Mostar paid special attention at having a presence around or in the vicinity of the hospital in order to dissuade the Armija from using mortars as from there. When we identified a mortar in the vicinity of the hospital, we in fact let this be known, and you were well-aware of this. I don't know if it happened more than once. As I said yesterday, you can set up a mortar, fire, and leave very quickly and there's hardly any traces left, but that's what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. I don't want to pursue the point. I just remain by the fact that it says in the reports preventing -- attempts to prevent, trying to prevent. Now another document from the Prosecution binder. P -- but before that, could you take this map over to the witness. P 06214. P 06214. P 06214. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. It's Madrid Task Force INTREP, date 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. You were there then. As a comment here -- look at the comment -- or, rather, before the comment, before the Jablanica section and point 3 that refers to Jablanica, it says here that the personnel of the BiH army said that they had very little work during the last few days. This piece of information confirms that for the moment the area is calm, as was reported in previous intelligence reports. End of comment. And then a sentence that I'm particularly interested in. "The Mostar children are continuing to offer the Spanish patrol all forms of military objects, including weapons." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll skip the portion about the hospital and the relatively calm situation at the time. Now, my penultimate question, and the map will be my last question, tell me how you comment the sentence from the report which says: "The Mostar children are continuing to offer the Spanish patrol all types of military objects, including weapons." And this refers to East Mostar. To the best of your knowledge, were there so many weapons that were out of control that it was even in the hands of children who offered it to the Spanish Battalion for them to buy, to buy off them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no sale of weapons to SpaBat, because SpaBat did not buy weapons from either side. The East Mostar patrol, as has been said on a number of occasions --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, please. Just a moment. I cooperated with SpaBat excellently, and I highly praise -- or was highly cognisant of the role that they were playing, and they were in a war that had nothing to do with their people. I'm quite clear about that, and I don't doubt for one moment that a Spanish officer wouldn't buy anything like that, but the question is very simple. I'm just referring to the situation in Mostar. Witness, sir, I can't use your rank, we had information about the Spanish Battalion. We know all about it, the extraordinary work they did, how much effort of they put into their work and so on, but here it says the Spanish children -- the Mostar children are continuing. It's the continuous tense. It doesn't say that members of the SpaBat bought the weapons, but it says that the children continued to offer them all sorts of military object, including weapons. So that refers to the overall situation. And as far as I'm concerned and the Trial Chamber is concerned, it's very important to arrive at something which is called the state of affairs, the situation on the ground as it actually was in all its entirety, which includes this fact, the fact that children are in possession of weapons. So do you know anything about that, and can you testify about this report and to what the report says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can go on with my answer, then the children in Mostar who were always near the Spanish patrol because we lived for a long time on the streets and our vehicles were permanently surrounded by -- rather, very frequently surrounded by children, particularly at the beginning, and offered the children, that is, soldiers, objects which they had picked up from around there. They have given us grenades and even on occasions some weapons. The attitude of the SpaBat in such cases was not to accept the objects and to entrust and beg the Armija, and because of the very danger that these objects represented for the children, to increase their vigilance. As you can imagine, fragments of grenades in East Mostar, well, there was plenty of that. Where the weapons could come from or where a child could have found a weapon, well, perhaps from some of the victims or from the houses. I don't know. But this did happen, and particularly at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Would you now take a look at the map on the ELMO. On the overhead projector there's a map that I provided. Take a look at it now, please. And this is the last thing I want to ask you. Once again, this is a Google image, or satellite image accessed through Google. The thick line is part of the Neretva River. Towards the north you see the airfield, the airport down below, and the HVO line. Well, I'm going to ask you if it's the HVO line. Now, up at the top -- well, you said you knew the positions of the army of Republika Srpska. Now, when you look at this map - this is my question - did the BH army to the best of your knowledge control the area between this left line and the positions of the HVO and the light line which is the position of the -- positions of the army of Republika Srpska? So that's my last question. To the best of your knowledge, the area in between, between these two lines, between these two lines drawn in there on the map, was it under BH army control while you were there, during the period that you were there? Of course the HVO army was there, but I think that what I'm asking is quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question quite clearly. I don't know whether my answer can be as accurate, because once again, General, we followed our own itineraries. As you well know we entered East Mostar through the airport route. We had to cross the runways, and then we took a track that led us to East Mostar. This, of course, included a large track of land controlled by the HVO. We crossed there the HVO lines then. We turned towards the north or north-east. There were a couple of kilometres of no man's land, and then we came into the armija-controlled territory . From there to the south or these two lines on the Neretva that you mark as the Serb border, well, we did not move around there until the peace agreement was signed and the weapons pick-up points were decided upon. From the north of the airport towards East Mostar, I can repeat what I said before. From East Mostar to the north, yesterday I said I don't know how far the HVO-controlled territory extended to, but to the north of Potoci and the river we saw HVO people. To what an extent they controlled the area, well, that's very difficult for me to say anything concrete when this comes to saying how -- to what extent they had military control. I'm terribly sorry, this is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, about streams and things like that and that there might have been the HVO there, well, let's leave that for the time being, although in your report you state the positions of the army of Republika Srpska. But anyway, thank you for the answers that you were able to give. Bon voyage to you. Thank you to the Trial Chamber, and that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Witness. I'd like to say good morning to everyone in the courtroom first and say at the outset to the Trial Chamber that we did not have an agreement with the Praljak Defence for them to use about 4/6th of the time allotted to the Defence. So I ask for the Trial Chamber's understanding as far as the requirements of General Petkovic is concerned. If you consider my questions to be relevant to the proceedings and if the Prosecution won't need more time for redirect, then I would like to request that you allow me more than half an hour to cross-examine this witness. And can you tell me how much more time the Defence has?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note 4/6th of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Accused Praljak used two hours, so normally you should have 30 minutes since nobody gave you any time. It's somewhat easier today. We have more time. So -- oh, who gave you time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody gave General Praljak any time either. At least that wasn't declared in the court room. And when we're talking about time, I consider that the time which one Defence does not wish to use up is not the property of that Defence so that that Defence can then cede its time to someone else, but then that time enters into something which is left to those who wish to avail themselves of it. I'll do my best to finish my cross-examination within one hour. If not, then I would request an extra 10 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ceded my time yesterday to the Defence teams who wish to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we now only have Mr. Petkovic's Defence counsel who would like to have an hour. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I omitted or, rather, I remembered straight away but you moved on. At one point in time when you referred to the witness, spoke to the witness, you used a word that I don't think you should have used. You mentioned his rank. You addressed him by rank. There was question about maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I know. I know. We've noticed it. We shall do something about it right away. Why don't you begin, and we'll have a break in 20 minutes' time and resume after that. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin, I'd just like to tell the Presiding Judge that I consider that I do have one hour's time and that I will perhaps request additional time in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Witness, I'd like to take this rare opportunity of having (redacted) in the courtroom here today to clarify some details from the aspects of military doctrine that you are very familiar with. So I'm going to ask you some general questions to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I didn't object yesterday, and obviously we're in the Trial Chamber's hands on what's ultimately decided, but as has already been observed, the witness has been brought largely as -- as a fact witness. He's not been designated as an expert witness by the Prosecution and certainly hasn't been classified in that way procedurally under the rules that apply to experts. Now, clearly the witness is in a position of knowledge in respect of general issues such as military doctrine and international humanitarian law, but if the witness is going to be taken beyond the scope of his testimony on direct, certainly I limited myself to what is, I think, more correctly viewed as factual information, but I think in some respect it's unfair now to take the witness and make him something other than what he was brought here for. I don't know whether the Spanish government has a position on that, but it's certainly an issue I think that merits some consideration before we proceed down this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I propose that I ask my question first and then if Mr. Stringer really objects and considers that my question goes beyond the examination-in-chief and the documents prepared for this witness, well, I'm reasonable enough to withdraw my question if that be the case. But until then, I suggest that you allow me to go ahead with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Raised by Mr. Stringer is a valid one. He's quite right. The examination-in-chief of the witness did not relate to those issues which you wish to raise, but you can on the basis of the question of a document of SpaBat address an issue of a military nature. Then you are able to meet your objective it. It's for you to handle the questions. Why don't you begin, and then we'll take from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I intended to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we start off by agreeing, and I think that we can agree, that East Mostar was defended in 1993 and 1994, and those the years that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when you asked me "That's a question," my answer was yes, and then we had the witness's answer. It wasn't recorded. So my answer to that is yes, it is a question. Now, can you answer my question whether Mostar, East Mostar, in 1993 and 1994 was defended? East Mostar, in 1993 and 1994, was defended. Was it a defended part of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, affirmative. Could I see the transcription on the screen, because I can't see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Witness, that East Mostar was defended by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that in East Mostar the 4th Corps had its headquarters as did the 41st Brigade of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me when I say that in East Mostar there were the members of the 41st Brigade there of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many soldiers as a rule a brigade numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. It varies a lot in different armies. And you ask about -- if you ask about the officers or the soldiers in this particular brigade, I must say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know how many members of that brigade at the material time was located precisely in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in East Mostar the BH army, did it have its military police? Witness, if you don't know, we'll move on to the next question. I can well believe that you can't remember 14 years on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Tell me, the Muslim authorities in East Mostar, did they have a civilian police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the Muslim authorities, did it have civilian protection or have you ever heard of the term that was referred to as civilian protection within the frameworks of the armed forces and defence of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the concept "targeted defence."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, civilian defence in East Mostar, interpreter's correction. Civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was -- I think there was a mistake. Not targeted defence. [In English] Civilian protection. [Interpretation] Civilian protection which is an organised force within the frameworks of the defence of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about that? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we agree that in East Mostar the BH army had mortars and other weapons? Artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the BH army in East Mostar undertook certain actions, military actions, against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that if there was an armed conflict and -- between both factions there were constantly military actions against one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, General Praljak started asking you about the legitimacy of military targets, and His Honour Judge Trechsel intervened with the observation that that was a legal issue, a legal matter. Now, I would like to ask you several questions in that regard, and could you please answer my questions exclusively from the aspects of Spanish observers in Mostar during that period of time, and yours and their grounds for concluding about the war conflict, which in a way you supervised. Did you consider that the command of the enemy army is a legitimate target of attack of the opposing army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't supervising the armed conflict. The commander of an army can be obviously a legitimate target of an attack. And to say that it can be -- sorry, it can be a military objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the grounds for making your conclusions in the reports that we've already read and ones that we're going to read through. Did you consider that some warehouse, depot, any other facility used by an enemy army a legitimate target of attack of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: A depot of -- an armed depot can be a military objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you consider that a mortar position of the enemy army is a legitimate target of attack of the opposite army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clearly a military objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Witness, that the rule for deploying a mortar, for using a mortar, is that they change positions a lot during a day, and after several shots they change positions because they are easily detectable? You can detect what positions were used to fire from. So they move their positions and thus prevent the enemy from destroying that mortar position. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the normal use.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if in a relatively brief period of time a mortar is deployed in different locations, can we consider that every one of these locations where the mortar had been is a legitimate military target for attacks by the opposing army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very ambiguous question because it depends on the intention of that fire, on all areas. This is another point of the terrain that can have a military interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. So sorry to interrupt. Mr. President, it's about time for the break, and during the break I would ask for permission to consult with the representative of the Spanish government to see if there are any objections or concerns on the part of the government in view of the fact that the witness is now really being made an expert. Let me just add I'm happy to do that in the presence of a representative of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do object even to that proposal. The witness does have the benefit of a representative of his government. That representative, as I understand it, is an eminently qualified individual and no doubt can stand right now, with Your Honours' leave, and address the Court or intervene in the proceedings with your leave if he has any concerns as to the focus of questions. But for the -- my learned friend to act, as it were, as an agent provocateur to get somebody to stand up and raise objectives that he has made himself in these proceedings is simply unnecessary in my submission. So I do object, with the greatest of respect, on the grounds of it simply being unnecessary in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put the question directly to the representative it of the Spanish government. The Defence is putting questions which are of a technical military nature, also relating to international law issues, the laws of war. She's asking questions about military targets, protection of civilians. In other words, legal issues, and these are technical questions which are being asked to a military man. Now, does the representative of the Spanish government object to this or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RECHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm convinced that my government would be and will be and will put at your disposal military experts or experts on international law that you might request. The witness has come here as a witness obviously, and the order that I have received is that as far as possible his statement should be limited to facts, observed facts, and not to carry out an expert analysis from a military or legal viewpoint. I think that my answer is clear enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall put a question to the witness. I have read your resume and I realised that you attended military training courses like any military man in an army of any country. Now, as an army officer, when an army officer is being trained, is an army officer trained about any military technical aspects which might arise whilst fighting? Are you -- can you shoot at a mortar in the vicinity of a house for instance. All these aspects which could be addressed by a military expert. So during your training have you been informed about all of this or has nothing been said about these things? In short, if you need to -- do you need to be a military expert in order to be able to answer these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the training of an officer, we learn how to use and to know about the limitations of force according to international law and according to all international conventions, and the rest you learn with practice and with -- and with help, but it is part of the officer's training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will now have a 20-minute break. We shall deliberate on the matter, and we'll tell you what our position will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. [Spanish interpretation on English channel] Relating to international humanitarian law and the laws of war, the Trial Chamber was advised by Defence counsel of General Praljak to put a number of questions to the witness which had not been put during the examination-in-chief. The Trial Chamber has noticed that the OTP has raised an objection by stating that its examination-in-chief did not relate to these questions. In addition, the Prosecution has also added that this witness benefits from protective measures, and therefore the -- his answers should be vetted by the representative of his government. The representative of the Spanish government let us know that the Spanish government was ready to cooperate and send a witness who could answer these questions but that the current witness could not answer these questions. Therefore, the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule -- Rule 90(H) of the Rules, the Trial Chamber recalls that 90(H)(i), the cross-examination is restricted to those issues raised during the examination-in-chief pertaining to the credibility of the witness and pertaining to the case of the party cross-examining the witness. When a party cross-examines a witness who is able to testify about a question relating to its case, it should have available elements which contradict the evidence if the Trial Chamber deems it fit can authorise questions to be put on other subjects. The Trial Chamber has noticed that this witness is a 92 ter witness, and we therefore have two written statements by this witness. The Trial Chamber feels that the questions put should not be beyond the scope of these two written statements. Now, as to know whether the Defence teams might be entitled to put questions beyond the scope of the statements, the Trial Chamber has decided not to grant the Defence application. Therefore, Ms. Alaburic, you may put question on the basis of the written statements and on the basis of the answers provided during the examination-in-chief. And as far as any other aspects are concerned, these other aspects can be dealt with with other witnesses. So that said, you now have 50 minutes left approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Trial Chamber, but I have already completed the set of questions that I intended to address to this witness, and now I'm going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us talk a bit about HVO attacks at members of UNPROFOR. Could you please have a look at a document -- or, rather, before that could I just remind you of your statement yesterday, recorded on page 36 of the transcript, that UNPROFOR was not a target -- or, rather, an objective of HVO attacks but that sometimes it was a target because it was in the area of combat activities. I would like to remind you of that statement of yours, and now I would like to ask you to look at document P 05883. That is a document from the Prosecutor's set of documents. And if I followed Judge Trechsel's remarks correctly as to where what document was, I think it should be in the second binder. So the document is P 5883. Could we please have a look at item 6 straight away. In item 6 it says that after the meeting -- it pertains to the 14th of October, 1993, that is. After the meeting at the headquarters of the 4th Corps, two members of the Spanish units were wounded. I am interested in the following comment, that HVO shelling was provoked by two mortar shells fired from BH army positions. Tell me, Witness, the document that I am referring to now, is it one that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about this incident and about this comment that it was a provoked attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commentary refers to the fact that when the chief of the unit was entering the Mostar municipality, he saw two Armija mortar shells being fired and after which then some mortar shells from HVO landed where I was. Sorry, not where I was but where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just clarify whether it was the entrance to the Mostar municipality or the command of the 4th Corps, since the meeting was held with representatives of the 4th Corps. I must admit that it was my understanding that it was at the 4th Corps command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm attempting to recall, and the paragraph says, that at the meeting at the 4th Corps the -- it was at the city hall entrance that this wound -- the two wounded occurred. And then the chief met with the municipality as well as with his counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the command of the 4th Corps was located at that municipality building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was at his own headquarters, I believe. I cannot actually say that with certainty. I seem to recall that it was two separate buildings. There was the headquarters of the 4th Corps and the municipality of Mostar, two separate buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, this municipality building, was it in the densely populated part of East Mostar or was it a lone building so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it was located to the south but within the actual city of Eastern Mostar, although more to the south of our own base but still within the actual city -- within the city of Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to ask you whether it was in the densely populated area of East Mostar, or was it somewhere in an isolated place far away from places where many people would gather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I recall that it was in the central section of Eastern Mostar, which was as populated as the rest of the city. It was in the centre of the city. It wasn't in an outlying position at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether that was the street of Marshal Tito, the one that you discussed yesterday with General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the question to be repeated. He didn't get the whole question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I repeat the question. Do you know that that building of the municipality was opposite the building where the 4th Corps command was and that both facilities were in the street of Marshal Tito?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot indicate whether that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, could you please tell us whether you were aware of efforts or attempts made by HVO commanders to inform their military units and caution them that they should not attack UNPROFOR patrols or any members of UNPROFOR or other international organisations, and what kind of measures they took for some incidents that indeed did take place to not be repeated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of internal HVO orders. It is obvious that there were attacks against UNPROFOR, and these happened with a certain frequency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have prepared here six documents. The Trial Chamber can have a look. And I'm not going to ask you about these documents that have to do with internal orders of the HVO because you said that you were not aware of that. So that would be a waste of time on my part. Witness, now I would like to clarify some details concerning shellings. Yesterday, you told us that patrols in East Mostar followed incoming and outgoing shells and other explosions. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As for West Mostar, you told us that it was only in March 1994 that a permanent base was established, a permanent UNPROFOR base in West Mostar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Up until that period, if I heard you correctly, there were patrols of the Spanish battalion that came to Western Mostar from Dracevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat what I've said, and that is that at every day we conducted -- we attempted to conduct a morning and evening patrol, afternoon patrol, up to dusk in Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us quite literally that the patrol would come to West Mostar early in the morning, that it would be there until lunch and then it would go back to Dracevo and come back in the afternoon and then go back to Dracevo yet again in the early evening. Was that the pace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned to Dracevo in order to prepare their meal, and right after their lunch they would western to Western Mostar until dusk.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the basis of what you said to us just now, one may conclude that part of the evening and the entire night were not covered by patrols by the Spanish Battalion in West Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many times in the day time as well because we weren't authorised to enter Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. The documents that were prepared for your testimony showed that the patrol in East Mostar had the task of following incoming and outgoing shells in East Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Also, it seems obvious that in West Mostar your patrol was supposed to follow outgoing and incoming shells in West Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. Anybody who would heard incoming or outcoming shell fire would attempt to identify the point, the precise time, after which this information was confirmed with the various parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Since your patrol in West Mostar was not in West Mostar during part of the evening and at night, it follows that in West Mostar there were no members of your units who in that locality would be able to follow the incoming and outgoing shells.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were not present, obviously they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If some reports from SpaBat contain information about shells shot during the night and which fell or were shot in West Mostar, fired in West Mostar, does that mean that the patrol from East Mostar would report on those shells and on that firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this patrol in East Mostar which was in the parking lot that you discussed at length with the general in Marsal Tito Street, and the members were either in the APC or if there was fine perhaps on top of the APC, did they in view of your knowledge of the locality, were they able visually or could they hear the firing of shells in West Mostar or shells which fell on West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that our patrol had a parking area in the Marsal Tito, but they weren't always there. They also moved around the city. And there could be many explosions in Western Mostar that they didn't necessarily see nor hear as -- as a patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, from that parking lot you can't see West Mostar, can you? You can have no visual contact with it, can you? From Marsal Tito Street, of course, because of the surrounding buildings. You can't see West Mostar from Marsal Tito Street, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: From some points on Marsal Tito Street you cannot see Western Mostar. There are some crossroads or streets that do allow you to see Western Mostar. And I want to repeat that the patrol was not just in the arcades of the Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the patrol -- were they in the vehicle that was moving and produced sounds -- [Spanish on English channel] on the basis of listening alone establish whether in West Mostar there was some shells falling or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the question be repeated, please. It hasn't been completely heard. The witness is now answering but has not heard the full question. This is the interpreter speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that the patrols were not in the parking lot all the time but that they would move round East Mostar; right? Drive around East Mostar. A moving vehicle creates sounds, does it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: People in a vehicle which is moving, as rule, cannot hear what is going on in their surroundings as well as somebody who is outside a vehicle. That would be right, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the conclusion. Members of the patrol who were in the vehicle or in vehicles that were moving would have found it more difficult to hear and, therefore, establish whether some shells were falling on West Mostar or not. Can we agree there with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do agree with that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'd like us now to clarify, I hope once and for all, the subject of the hospital and some other localities which are linked to the shelling. So can we go through the Prosecution documents very quickly and see what happened? May we look at document P 5899 first, please. It's the same document, the one we had just a moment ago. And the entry for the 15th of October says that actions to uncover whether the BH army has mortar positions near its hospital, not will be continued. I'm going to list all the documents first, Witness, in which the hospital is mentioned. I don't think there's any need for us to waste time opening each of these documents, but I will mention the section of the document where this is mentioned if someone wants to check it out. So the other documents produced by the Prosecutor mentioning the hospital is this: P 5954, and that's a report for the 19th of October, and it says that SpaBat still -- is still attempting to do away with Muslim mortars in the -- in the plural, that's my comment, near the hospital. Is trying to get rid of the Muslim mortars near the hospital. Now, the third document is this: P 6163, for the 26th and -- the 27th of October, 1993. Also on page 3. SpaBat is still attempting to prevent the presence of Muslim mortars in the vicinity of the hospital. And the fourth document, which is in the second binder, relates to the 16th of November, 1993, and it is to be found on page 4 where it says -- well, the document is P 06688. Let me repeat the document number. P 06688. And it's in the first Prosecution binder. It is a report for the 16th of November, and on page 4 it says as follows: "SpaBat is trying to prevent the laying -- the positioning of Muslim mortars near the hospital." Now, the fifth document is P 7256. It is a report for the 19th of December, 1993. Page 3 which says: "SpaBat is continuing to try and prevent the Muslims from placing mortars near the hospital." And I think that will suffice, Witness, for us to reach a conclusion. Witness, can you confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, in respect of reading into the record of the numbers of exhibits that aren't going to be shown to the witness, I'm recalling the Trial Chamber's decision that it issued last June. It was a special decision in respect of witnesses who appear under Rule 92 ter, and at the time the Trial Chamber reminded the Prosecution that even in respect of Rule 92 ter witnesses, if it wants to tender documents into evidence through such a witness, the documents need to be shown to the witness. And I understand the time constraints that counsel's facing. I face them also. And obviously I could stand and read into the record the numbers of lots of other very interesting and useful Spanish Battalion documents without showing them to the witness in order to get them into the record and to get into the record information that's contained in them, but I didn't do that. And so it's our position, and it will be that we're going to object to the admission of any documents tendered by the Defence that are not shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic. You've mentioned some documents, 6688, 7256. Have they been admitted into evidence or not? Because indeed there are two problems. There is the admission of the documents and then the way you go about them. 7256, that is been admitted yet or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, these are not documents which I prepared to go with this witness. They are documents prepared by the Prosecution to put to this witness. And since the witness in his own statement spoke about mortar positions of the BH army in the vicinity of the hospital in point 60, paragraph 60, and we discussed this matter in this courtroom before this witness, it was not my intention to show Prosecution documents in order to tender those documents in any way. Most of those documents, as my colleague Mr. Stringer -- well, he showed the documents to the witness yesterday. All I'm interested in is an answer to the question. How long, to the best of his knowledge, did the Spanish Battalion exert pressure on the Muslim side to refrain from positioning mortars or mortar positions in the vicinity of the hospital. That's all. Now, I agree that the documents speak for themselves and it is not my intention to tender Prosecution documents with this witness, but I quoted the document numbers because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 and 7, I think, that the Defence asked how long the SpaBat exerted pressure on the ABiH for them to remove their mortars, the mortars that were in the vicinity of the hospital. So either you know or you don't know. So please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know the answer, Your Honour. I think that I spoke about this yesterday as well. And as to the reason why this is mentioned so many times in the SIT reports and the INTREPS, or SITREPS, sorry, the reason is because the patrol received the order, the patrol in Mostar received the order to count incoming and outgoing shell-fire, and also received the order to maintain a proximity, presence, near the hospital in order to avoid the Armija deploying or placing mortars in the vicinity of the hospital. So this is a novelty basically, and we continue thus deterring the Armija from placing or firing or located mortars in the vicinity of the hospital. It was a permanent mission, we can say, and that is why this is referred to in the reports. How long? Throughout the whole mission this is what we did. Just like we conducted the patrols, we yesterday took a look and saw what the mortar situation was. It doesn't mean that every day we found mortars, eh. But when we did see mortars we would report it, we'd tell the Armija. We'd tell them you cannot locate mortars here and we'd the HVOs as well, we sometimes would found mortars near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like us to take a look at two documents and then we'll comment on them. The first document, once again in the Prosecution binder, the second binder, in fact. The number of the document is P 07408. And it deals with the section East Mostar. So the first point for East Mostar, under the heading "East Mostar," P1, it says: "The BH army positioned various mortar positions in town which are used at random. They position mortars, they are firing shells, and then they change their positions." Tell us, please, the report is indeed a report from SpaBat; right? Did you have knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of this report, and it's an official SpaBat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
