utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you knew about the situation? I mean, the placing of mortar positions, random use of mortars, firing shells, then changing positions, the position of the mortars. You personally, did you have the information and knowledge about that? And all this in reference to East Mostar. It all has to do with East Mostar, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have knowledge of the contents of this paragraph saying that there were positions set up so as to receive mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's take a look at another document, once again a Prosecution document in that same binder. The number is P 7771. It is also for East Mostar. Under B, point 3, referring to East Mostar. It says that the shelling by the HVO in recent days mostly focused on the area between the hospital, the 4th Corps, the SpaBat patrol, and the Presidency, and that is an area where most of the people usually gather out in the streets. Now, in view of that observation by SpaBat, I would like to ask you the following: As we've just seen that the BH army had mortar positions near the hospital, part of the 4th Corps subject and legitimate targets we've dealt with. Now, can you tell us, did the BH army really place its mortar positions in the parts of town where you people usually gathered out in the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about Marsal Tito Street. I never saw a mortar located on Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Marsal Tito Street. Let's concentrate on the facilities here. The hospital is mentioned. The 4th Corps is mentioned. And we have already seen documents according to which there was a mortar position that launched -- that provoked an HVO attack which was, as you said, near the Mostar municipality buildings -- or, rather, opposite the 4th Corps. So in that part of town. And that is indeed Marsal Tito Street. But then we also mentioned hospital close to which were the mortar positions. So I'm now asking you in that connection whether those localities for which we have already established that there were mortars placed there, were these locations places where large numbers of civilians would gather in the street? That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've spoken about seeing mortars in the vicinity of the hospital. In the whole Eastern Mostar area there were places prepared for mortars, and the preparation for a mortar is basically a small ramp on the floor so that you can then set up the basic plate, which is a piece of equipment. It's a steel plate where the tube is leaned upon. There is nothing more to it than that. On highly populated streets it is difficult to shoot a mortar because you are screened out by the buildings. You have to have an open front to shoot from. And if you told me that there were mortars here, I frankly don't know. Neither do I know from where the Armija was shooting each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question is extremely relevant. We have a SpaBat document which I'm discovering with you. This is document 7458, and it says that the ABiH, has positioned mortars in the city, randomly fires from them and then removes them. That is the observation made by SpaBat. In such a situation on the HVO side, and this is why I need your military expertise, the HVO has learnt that there's just been fire, fire from this zone. Because as you explained, a piece -- a plate of metal has been put on the ground with the tube on top of it. So the HVO learned that there's just been fire from a given point, and the information is communicated through their own channel. In order to put an end to the firing, an order may be given for counter-fire. This is -- it could be from a tank. That is a hypothesis. For from another mortar or through another piece of weaponry. But all of this is going to take some time. There is going to be some delay in action. The mortar is removed, but the counter-fire may come at that time, a few minutes later, and it could happen, unfortunately so, that there would be civilians around on the spot. Such a scenario, can it be understood militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question cannot be answered lightly. I'll try to explain to you how mortars operate or how any artillery unit operates. It is put into position, it is fired, and then it is moved somewhere else. And during wartime, both the HVO and the Armija had many locations that they had previously prepared, and some of them were fixed locations. From those locations that had been prepared they could do two things. First, to move the mortars around rather than keep them as easy targets from enemy fire. And secondly, data, firing data obtained from each of those locations is obtained and then used to do more precise targeting if atmospheric conditions are favourable. So once you know a particular location, it is very easy to have a grid of targets that you can shoot against with precision, because you have already recorded and corrected your firing data previously. So in the area we're talking about where I had two of my people wounded, we're talking about Marsal Tito Street, and I said that I never saw a mortar location there. First of all, because as I said, there is a big building. Defence was asking me whether we could see Western Mostar. And while we said we couldn't see it, a mortar couldn't be shot from there. And I've said on several occasions that we did see mortar locations near the hospital. I said that the hospital is some 3 or 400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer. Please, General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] With Your Honour's permission, I'd like to ask the witness two questions. Witness, what are you by profession? Are you a tankist, a sailor, an infantryman? What would be your branch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an infantryman, sir. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Witness, according to your rules, NATO rules, for fighting in built-up areas it says that mortars are positioned behind buildings and thereby you have cover. Is that correct or not? It is Rule F105, I believe, of the NATO rules. Well, I studied them, and I know how you're supposed to act in built-up areas, and I know that mortars are always behind certain buildings or features so that they are hidden from view. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mortar characteristics normally needed to be used covered by some sort of protection, a building or something like that, but what you have to ensure is that the height of the building or whatever allows the shooting angle to be the right one. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Let me just inform you that I'm an artilleryman and I worked for 20 years as an artilleryman, 20 years as an instructor in military academies. So your -- I accept your explanation about mortars, but let me ask you this: If a mortar targets at a short distance, short range targets a target, and the other target is at a greater distance, and the difference being one and a half kilometres, where is the trajectory, longer or shorter? You know what a trajectory is, of course. And is it true that when a mortar shoots at a target which is at a closer distance, its trajectory is far higher, has to go higher, than when the target is at a greater distance when the trajectory is lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, obviously, General. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you. Now, Witness, I say, and you can confirm this, but I claim that the highest high-rise building in New York, if you were to position a mortar behind it we will be able to hit a target at a distance of three kilometres. Do you agree? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would depend on the mortar characteristics. In any case, I agree with you. I'd say it would not be easy in any way. In Marsal Tito Street I never saw any mortar emplacements. I do know that 300 metres away there were mortar emplacements. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Emplacements. I'm not asking whether you've seen anything like that. You were talking about the characteristics of a mortar. Let me ask you again. From a mortar position, the person doing the shooting, doing the targeting, can he see the target at all? He knows where it is, but does he see it? He can see it, but he needn't see it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right. Not necessarily. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] We're talking about mortars here, as a weapon, a piece to be used in built-up areas, most suited to built-up areas, because there are no obstacles regardless of the height of the building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically, yes, you could use a mortar. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you were following the number of shells falling on East or West Mostar, did you at the same time monitor events and analyse the war conflicts and war action between the BH army and the HVO in Mostar and the surrounding parts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you never tried to establish why, for example, in mid-October 1993 the number of shells that were fired was far greater than in the period prior to that and after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say with any certainty whether in October 1993 the number of shells was fewer than what I later saw, lived through, in November, December, particularly November. Yesterday, we saw some pictures or graphs perhaps that actually -- some graphs, actually, perhaps that could help us. But aside from that, I don't know why. I don't know about the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the charts for December 1993 and the first two months of 1994. Now, my associates have drawn up a detailed review of all your reports, and from those reports we can see exactly when the number of shells fired was greater than if we can put it this way, the usual number, and these facts and figures can be linked up to what was going on in the field. So since you didn't that a while you were in Mostar, let's try and do that now. Look at document -- look at a document in my own binder, my own set of documents. The number is P 4698, and it's an analysis by SpaBat about the situation in Mostar and Jablanica from April to September 1993. And at the very end of that document, on the last page, in fact, so on the last page, the last three paragraphs of that document contain something that I would like to discuss as an introduction to my next topic. One Tactical Group was exchanged by another. And since we're dealing with September 1993, tell me whether this was an exchange that referred to you, because you arrived in the area when an ATG was relieved. It's the last paragraph of this analysis. Very well. It doesn't really matter. Witness, let's see what it is in the last three paragraphs here. This is the situation in the area where you arrived and during the hand-over you had to be informed about the situation. I'll start reading, I quote "The preparations and the amassment of troops in the area were bigger by the day. In the area of Grabovica a large concentration of BiH forces from Sarajevo has been noted. Again in the area of Grabovica a large concentration of BiH forces from Sarajevo, Zenica, and the area of Konjic and Jablanica is taking place. "The best Armija unit, the 7th Muslim Brigade, incorporating a majority of Arab troops has been transferred to the area. An imminent attack is foreseen. The objective at first glance is to control the hills at Vrdi since with that the BiH army would secure the control of the Jablanica-Mostar road. The BH army carried out an offensive on Vrdi on the 14th of September. The HVO had to pull back from the area. A part of the Croatian forces remained in the pocket and their position is not good. There is no HVO reaction aimed at recapturing that important position." And in conclusion, "At the time of relief of one ATG by another, the situation in the area is that the BH army conducted a southward offensive from Vrdi to bring pressure on Mostar, and there was fighting in the Slatina-Doljani area. It is foreseeable that the southward operation will continue because this is principal BiH objective at the moment." Witness, during the hand-over of duties were you informed of this BiH offensive in the month of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about this, and I said that I must have had knowledge about this but that the practical repercussion for us was that convoys could not go along the routes we used to arrive at Jablanica and particularly along the Dreznica Valley. I then went on to say that I arrived at the area on the 23rd of September, and one of our companies was then ferried over 10 days before by air in order to take over from the unit stationed at Jablanica. We had a detachment there. That company could not go up up until the 21st. On the 21st the Mostar to Jablanica road was open because the 11th Company of SpaBat went there and took over from the unit until then stationed there. But once again the practical repercussions for us whose duty was to provide protection was that the road was closed. The solution of the conflict, as I said before, I know nothing about because we had no duties nor any possibilities of monitoring the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on, please, registrar, can you tell me how many minutes have been used by Ms. Alaburic? It must be something around an hour. No. You've used up 48 minutes, so you should have another 12 minutes. It's now five to 12.00. Mr. Stringer, how much time would you need for your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would say perhaps 15 to 20 minutes, Mr. President, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a few documents that originate from the BiH army. Those were issued before you arrived in the territory of Mostar. I will want to hear from you whether you were familiar with the behaviour of the BH army that are based on those orders. These orders are inter-related. Let's look at them in a sequence and then I will put the question to the witness. The first document in my binder again is 4D 00709. This is a general order by the commander of the 4th Corps, Arif Pasalic, issued on the 10th of September, 1993, to all the operations group that we already encountered in the documents shown to you by General Praljak. Let us focus on item number 4 in which the OG centre is ordered to focus their combat activities on the city of Mostar and the Hum feature in order to liberate the political, cultural, and economic centre of Herzegovina. Have you been able to locate the document, the document 4D 00709? Witness, have you been able to locate that document? Look at the yellow tabs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at paragraph 4 in the document. Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps, orders the OG centre to focus combat activities towards the town of -- and Hum with the goal of creating conditions to liberate the political, cultural, and commercial centre it of Herzegovina. Sir, can you agree with me that the reference here is being made to Mostar, that the town in question is Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is not receiving interpretation, I believe. It seems that the witness is not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me now? Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Can we agree, Witness, that item number 4 in this order refers to Mostar and the hilltop that is known under the name of Hum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at another document. The number is 3D 00740. Let's look at bullet point 3B. 3B. Again this was issued by Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps on the 15th of September. He issues a combat order and under item 3B he specifies the lines of combat activities. I would like to draw everybody's attention to the line that we are all familiar with. That's the Stotina-Hum line. And then in the last lines of this item a reference is made to an attack in the direction of Hum and Santiceva Street. Tell me, please, Santiceva Street is a street on the western bank of Neretva, that was the separation line between the Muslim and the Croat parts of Mostar. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether where that street is. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that the Trial Chamber is familiar with the street plan of Mostar and where Santiceva is. Now another document, 3D 00736. That will be the last document in this series. Let's look at bullet point number 2 in this document. A reference is made to an attack at the inner city centre in order to take the axes which are listed herein. And then bullet point number 4, please, where it says, "I've decided" -- and let's say who the author of the document is. The author is Commander Semir Terjovic [phoen]. "I have decided to carry out an attack by grouping the main forces on the axes," and he lists the axes, the first one is Hum facility left of Stotinja, Rodoc, Podum to the right, then second axes is the electric power plant of Mostar, Rastani, Orlovac, and the auxiliary forces on the axes, Santiceva Street, the old people's home. I don't know what "BNR" stands for. There is the Bulevar of People's Revolution, the grammar school, the health care centre, and the goal is to crush the enemy forces on the lines of advance of our forces inflicting losses in manpower, in technical equipment, and materiel, and at the same time to create conditions for launching final operations, the purpose of which would be the final liberation of town. My question to you is this, Witness: When you arrived in the area of Mostar, were you informed that approximately eight days before that a BiH army operation was launched in Mostar in order to liberate Mostar, as they put it, from the Ustashi forces again as they called those forces in their orders? Were you familiar with that operation of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot say with any certainty that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see what was happening towards the end of Mostar. Look at another document in my binder. 4D 00713. In the meantime an agreement was signed on cease-fire. Arif Pasalic on the 29th of September, 1993, issued an order on stopping all combat activities targeting HVO, and that should have taken effect on the 30th of September, 1993. Witness, let's look at bullet point 6 of that document, maybe you can clarify some things for us. The commander of the 4th Corps ordered his units to start opening fire or any other combat activity and at the same time in a certain way he seems to be apologising for having issued such an order to them. Therefore, in item 6 he says as follows: "Ensure strict fulfilment of this order because there are other reasons that influenced the passing of this decision." Witness, would you be able to provide us any explanation as to what is at stake here, why this order was issued in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at bullet point 5 where it says if HVO would -- were not to respect the agreement within the -- within the next 24 hours, you will get either a written or oral order to continue combat activities. Can we then agree that it is beyond dispute that before that the army of BiH had been opening fire and that they were ready to continue doing so if the cease-fire was not honoured. My question is would you agree that up to then the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was until then conducting certain offensive activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking for my opinion about documents which belong to the commands of the parts. What we did was to protect humanitarian aid because there's two factions in conflict. So I don't know all the details of the military operations, but both parties, and that is what you're asking me, well, the HIB was carrying out military action against the HVO was something I give for granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to put two questions to this witness. You mentioned the Medjugorje memorandum. Was it created on the following day, on the 4 -- 1st of October? Can you answer my question or not? In your statement you mentioned the Medjugorje memorandum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just checking. I'm just checking, General. It was signed the 2nd of October. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] And now I'm asking you this: If you're faced with an order issues by a commander who says on the 29th, i.e., on the 30th of September, you have to stop combat activities, you're a high-ranking officer. This document doesn't mean anything to you, and you're saying that the shells are falling. Witness, are we talking about a picnic here with the shells falling? Is this the reason why the shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to the question. The witness is testifying about things he knows. He's not going to give evidence and opinions clearly as to why shells might be falling. All he knows is that they are falling, and I think he's said that repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct. Please rephrase your question, General. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you. Witness, does it arise from this document, can you see in this document that the commander of the 4th Corps stopped the offensive by his forces in the town of Mostar both to the south and the north of him? Is there a sentence here, is there an item in this order where he orders that all combat activities had to stop? Can you see it in the document? Does this exist in the document or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to be more specific I need time to read it. I think this was an agreement. It was a declaration of intent, and I think that that's what it refers to. I can't really understand how -- what -- your question. I don't know. Either I don't understand your question or I don't have an answer to it. The parts make a special effort to protect civilian population. Each party will issue orders with the terms of this memorandum. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you about Medjugorje. I'm not asking you about Medjugorje. I'm asking you about the document that is in front you on the screen. Arif Pasalic's order to seize the offensive of the BiH army. This is what I'm asking you about. Is this an order? Is this a document that tells the BiH units to stop the offensive? You have to do it. Is this what the document says? I'm not asking you whether you knew about this document or not. I'm just asking you about the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic, the document says what the document says. I'm not going to interpret any document that hasn't been issued either by my chain of command or by myself. You know perfectly well what the document states. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. And just one more question, please. When my Defence counsel read to you the document that were drafted by your predecessors, the group that was there before you, my Defence counsel has provided you a document in which it says that your predecessors handed over the duties to you, and at about the same time the BiH army offensive was launched. Can you find that in that document? Was that part of that document, that a BiH army offensive was launched at the moment when you arrived and that you had been briefed about that by your predecessors. You -- albeit you didn't know about the extent of that offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat once again. I was briefed. I think I was briefed, although I can't remember that specifically, but I -- well, possibly, yes I was informed. Probably I was informed. But the practical effect that it had for us was that at least during a week the route towards Zelenica was closed as has happened in many other times while I was in Bosnia, because they were telling us about conflicts in Vrdi. Now, that was the consequence. The 21st that route was opened. On the 23rd we got there and on the 24th there was the handing over between both groups. So that was the consequence, the practical effect of this offensive if it existed because you know that we weren't controlling that. In East Mostar I didn't visit the front line or the armija's or yours. I didn't visit those lines. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I was really interested in the movement of yours and the problems that you had in your movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, normally speaking your time is up. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I would have a few more questions, and since mine learned friend Stringer said that he would need some 15 or 20 minutes, would I kindly ask you to give me another half an hour in which time I'm sure I would be able to complete my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have until 12.30. At 12.30, we shall give the floor to Mr. Stringer for his 15-minute redirect, and we shall stop at -- and adjourn at a quarter to 1.00. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave of you and your colleagues, I would ask for five minutes before the end of the day just to address one issue with you. It will take five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we analyse just one sentence of yours, because I was quite surprised by it. In answering my client's question, you used the words that the "BiH army offensive, if it existed at all, since you know that we did not control that," that's page 64, line 17, 18, 19 of the LiveNote, what I would like to know is this: If the Spanish Battalion was not controlling such combat activities how come that in the analysis that we just saw in document number P 0498, how come that it is recorded in the document that that BiH army concentrated its troops, carried out certain offensive activities and planned to carry out offensive towards the south of their theatre of war, i.e., towards Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you can show a -- show me a new document that I might not recall now, and maybe I have to give an opinion on another document, but in this document we talk about intentions of the Bosnian army that could be based on reports, intelligence reports, or communication between the parties, or it can either be information by UNPROFOR. So these are informations which are used to frame, so to speak, the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, let's move on. Let's move on. Can you please look at a document in the Prosecution -- Prosecutor's binder. P 6405. Let me just see whether it's in the first or the second binder. The second binder. This is a report for the 4th of November. You can listen to me. You don't have to follow the document. It's not important really. It says that Budakovic, BiH army commander, stated a few days before that that he wouldn't mind signing a deal with the army of Bosnian Serbs to fight Croats together. Witness, are you familiar with this name? Do you know who Mr. Budakovic was, Sulejman Budakovic? Did you ever hear of that person? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I have heard of him, but I don't remember that right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever hear, did you ever read in other Spanish Bat reports that BiH army commanders were ready to cooperate with the army of Republika Srpska against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, then, let me ask you few things about the siege of Mostar. Tell me, the siege of Mostar as a concept or a term or just a siege as a term, does it include a fact that a town is inaccessible, i.e., that you can't enter it or leave it? In military terminology would that be a fair definition of a siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In absolute terms, yes, a siege or a sieged city --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues] ... be a city that has all its way out or all its exits closed and no food and no other resources can get into that city. Although it is not a very modern concept.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In my binder can you please look at document P 4435. 4435 is the document which is a SpaBat report for the 22nd of August, i.e., before you arrived, but this is going to be my foundation for my next question. In the Spanish text the page, the first asterisk, and in the B/C/S version it's the end of the fifth page. It says in the record according to the statement of the BiH army in Jablanica, the majority of refugees from Capljina and Stolac who have been cut off in Mostar and Blagaj intend to return to Jablanica by using the roads through the mountains. My question is this your -- Witness: Were you familiar with the fact that Mostar, throughout all this time, including the time while you were there, was connected with Jablanica and that one could enter Mostar and one could leave Mostar using the mountain road that is mentioned in this SpaBat report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is in this report, and in my own statement I also refer to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, wasn't it precisely this mountain road that was used for supplying the BH army with ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did members of other BH army units come down that road in order to assist the 41st Brigade in Mostar, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't guarantee that information either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this document that we saw, we realised that people who were in Mostar wished to move to Jablanica. Did you know about people from East Mostar wanting to leave East Mostar and going into -- wishing to go to Jablanica as stated in this report? Did you have any knowledge about that? Did you ever hear of part of the inhabitants of East Mostar wishing to leave East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, yes. Quite easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we please have a look in my set of documents, 4D 00545. This is a small excerpt from Esad Sejtanic's book. 545. It is an excerpt from the book written by the commander of 42nd Brigade of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a very short excerpt. We can read it out actually. He is describing the situation in Mostar, and he says: "The situation in the town and its surroundings has become increasingly hard. Hunger was raging all around. The little food that was coming to Mostar from Jablanica via Glogova was distributed in driblets and again a large number of inhabitants wanted to leave for Jablanica and further on for Bosnia. By repressive measures regrettably we prevented the outflow of population and reduced any population movements to a minimum." Tell us, Witness, did you have any knowledge to that effect that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was interested in having as many civilians remain in East Mostar as possible irrespective of living conditions and conditions of waging war at that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now since I do not have more time, could we have a look at 4D 0072. 722 that is. 4D 00722. This is a report of Mr. Sulejman Budakovic that we mentioned a few minutes ago. It's from the end of August 1993. That's why -- I'm mentioning it here just to lay a foundation for my question. It has to do with UNPROFOR going to the eastern part of Mostar. It is a convoy that was discussed a great deal in this courtroom. In the second half of the first excerpt it says that: "Mr. Thornberry believes that with the assistance of a media campaign that will start in the world, the HVO will relent and allow food to be brought into the eastern part of town." And in conclusion, Mr. Budakovic says that: "In addition to media presentation and 300 kilogrammes of medicaments nothing was done, nothing was done apart from that." So my question will have to do with the media campaign and the media presentation. Tell me, did you ever witness the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Muslim authorities doing something even to the detriment of their own population, like keeping people who wanted to leave in East Mostar just in order to produce the desired media effect and to bring pressure to bear through foreign media on foreign governments and in turn in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you ever observe any such thing happening in the area that was under the control of the Muslim authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the additional time, although I would have been much more satisfied had I had more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't sure if the Trial Chamber wanted to take a break at this point or whether we were just going to continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you a couple questions and take you back to a few of the documents suggestions to put to the Court to the situation at Bijela bridge, and the first document was one that you were shown by the accused, General Praljak. It is number 3D 01089. It is the fourth document from the end of the thick stack of documents which I think is sitting there on the ELMO. Fourth from the end. Fourth. 1089.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 19th of October, 1993, and although it's not signed it's over the name of Milivoj Petkovic, Lieutenant General. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked quite a lot about the various positions, and this position or this location in particular in terms of whose control or which -- which of the parties was in a position to assert control over this location. Directing your attention to point number 2 in that, pursuant to this document of General Petkovic, it's indicated that the HVO units in the area will refrain from any military operations. Do you see that? "Operations that would disturb bridge construction."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph it's stated that the HVO will approve of the constant presence of the UN military observers in the HVO North Sector, sector all through the construction works for the bridge. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then moving down to item 6, the indication is that all HVO units will be given clear orders based on this approval.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Based on this, and based on what you recall, are you able to say whether the HVO was in a position to exert military control over the location of the Bijela bridge at this point in time, October 19, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said previously that I believe I recall that control to the Bijela bridge was indeed in the hands of the HVO. Maybe the western part of the Bijela bridge was not permanently occupied by anyone, but I think that it was possible to fire on that area from Bijela.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next document is in one of the Prosecution binders. It's in the binder on the chair there to your left, B2 binder. And the Exhibit number is 6568. P 06568. And is this -- General Praljak took you to this document. It's a document of the Spanish Battalion. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. It's an INTSUM of the rapid action force which was part of the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this one, I believe, is dated the 11th of November, 1993. General Praljak took you to a paragraph 2 here in which it's indicated that General Pasalic reported the destruction of the bridge. I'd like to take you actually to the paragraph that precedes that in which it's indicated that General Praljak announced he would not allow reconnaissance of the Bijela bridge until the highest authorities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had committed themselves in writing that the road would only be used for humanitarian purposes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Based on that Spanish Battalion document and perhaps your own recollection, do you know whether General Praljak was in a position to exert through the HVO military control over the Bijela bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were able to exert a certain degree of control over the Bijela bridge, and what arises from here is fear on the part of HVO that it might be difficult to separate humanitarian convoys from military traffic at the bridge location. So there was a degree of prevention on a military basis, and of course, concern about re-establishing this route.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is in the same binder. It's Exhibit number 7283. And I'm looking at page 5 of the English translation under the heading of point 5, "Other information." Point 5 relates to other information. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And item number 4 indicates that a patrol of the Spanish Battalion going to carry out work at the bridge came under fire from the west side. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the west side. Is that what you said, west side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you see that indicated in the report under item 4? 5 should say -- item 5, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: West side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now -- and I believe you indicated a few minutes ago it was your recollection, was it not, that it was HVO units that exerted control over the west side or the western half of this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at these coordinates, and when we conducted reconnaissance, we were fired upon in the armoured cars or the tyres of such cars as we went from East Mostar toward the Bijela bridge. We would be fired on from a house located on the western side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during your cross-examination yesterday by General Praljak, you indicated -- you said, "We were shot at intensely by HVO troops. You may well ask why I saw HVO troops. Well, because I saw them with my own eyes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment yesterday I was referring to this point, which I believe is slightly to the north of Potoci, and at the entrance to Mostar it was obvious that we were being fired upon from the HVO-occupied airport facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then just to close off that item then, Witness, at the end of his cross-examination General Praljak informed you that he'd cooperated excellently with the Spanish Battalion. So I'd like to ask for your assessment on that. In respect of the Bijela bridge, did the HVO and General Praljak cooperate excellently in respect of the construction at the bridge and making it work?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that this is a misinterpretation of General Praljak's question and answer. We -- he did not say "We had excellent cooperation Mostar-Bijela bridge." He was referring generally to the cooperation they had while he was there. This is impermissible to put misinterpreted words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's a fair question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have a look at the transcript. Praljak's question in the transcript is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that General Praljak did put questions on the relationship he had with the Spanish Battalion, so as part of these relations, perhaps Mr. Stringer could address the question in greater detail. So please put your question, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, could you give us your assessment, your own assessment, of the level of HVO cooperation in respect of the Bijela bridge project? And if you can comment specifically the level of cooperation you saw or experienced on the part of Generals Praljak and Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms I must start by saying or, rather, repeating that our relations with the parties is something that was not under my competence but something under the general competence of the task force commander. During our presence there, our relation were as cordial as possible with both parties, and our cooperation was as close as possible with both forces as well. Now, as to the efficiency of the cooperation, that is a judgement that I do not wish to take a stand on. I cannot actually make a judgement on that on something that I really do not know how it took place or what the reasons were to prevent such cooperation to take place. So therefore I must limit myself to the facts and maybe concerning the second part in cooperation at the Bijela bridge. The general authorised reconnaissance. I believe it was on the 16th of October. We were told that reconnaissance and the necessary studies would be authorised, but as far as the rebuilding of the bridge, that would have to take place later on due to military reasons. We worked at the bridge. We attempted to clean the area. As I said, we cleared some mine. We prepared access to the future bridge. We did have some incidents, for example, when we actually responded there. We were fired upon on various occasions, and sometimes while actually working on the bridge we were fired upon sporadically, and we were not able to find a solution to crossing the Bijela River until the month of March where the solution was a sort of an on and off type of solution. We had to establish a base there and build a pontoon which was then used to cross to both sides of the river and carry the convoy vehicles without having to go round. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me direct your attention now to Exhibit 5883. That's also in binder B2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, Mr. Stringer, let me tell you that we have still six minutes for the tape. Mr. Khan is going to need a few minutes. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the count -- by our count is that the Defence got a combined total of three and a half hours for cross-examination compared to my two hours, so I'm doing my -- I'm doing my best, but I think that the situation is not one that's the most equitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the point. I was just drawing your attention to this. We could have a break and then resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That would be fine. If Mr. -- I can continue or we can take a break now, whichever the Trial Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Judge Prandler has other commitments so there is just the two of us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to take you back to P 7283. 7283 is in the binder B2. Before the break this was the one we were looking at which had the reference to the patrol that was fired upon at the Bijela bridge, but I wanted to ask you a couple other things about this one as well. First of all, this one's dated 20th of December. It's a Spanish Battalion INTSUM, 392, and there's a reference in -- in section -- well, at the beginning about East Mostar, and on this date it indicated that there had been 315 prisoners released from Rodoc to East Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would this have been a prisoner release or a prisoner transport that the unit you were attached to would have been involved with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably us who were involved with them. There's mention of transport in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during the course of your tour --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I didn't want to interrupt my learned friend. However, I would be interested in whether my learned friend could tell us. I don't remember that any questions have been put to the witness during any of the cross-examinations on that particular topic. Could my learned friend maybe remind us of the question that has been put about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any question as to the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it's a valid point, Mr. President. I'm going to get there. I'm going to ask the witness to note this and to note one other thing in this report, and then ask the witness a question that will fall, I believe, very squarely within the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you could just note here there was a witness release on that day. Prisoners were released, and they were then transported into East Mostar. And then -- setting that aside and then turning the page of the English translation to item 3 -- sorry, item 4. Now there's a reference on the same day to 43 explosions that were registered in East Mostar, as well as two outgoing rounds. Okay. So now this is my question: Did you and other members of your unit observe shelling activities in East Mostar occurring at the same time that large numbers of prisoners were being brought into East Mostar after they'd been released from the HVO prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a specific answer. Every time convoys arrived we also had to know how many shellings there had been, but I don't think there was a co-relation, a cause-and-effect relation between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did the two -- the two events, that is prisoner releases into East Mostar and shelling of East Mostar, did those two things happen in parallel throughout the period of your tour in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The release of prisoners primarily took place in the month of December, and the unilateral releases and exchanges took place at that time. Now, as to the shellings, that would change from 20 to 100 throughout the duration of our mission, and I do not recall bearing in mind a cause-and-effect correlation between the arrival of prisoners to East Mostar and an increase in the HVO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked about how well members -- you and members of your unit who were doing the patrols in East Mostar, how well they could hear the -- the incoming or the outgoing rounds of artillery if they were actually driving around in an armoured vehicle. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to explain that we weren't always inside the vehicle, neither were all of the patrol members driving around the city. We had some people at the base entrance when we did have one. We had people in the parking lot. Sometimes we'd go to visit the hospital. So we had people who sometimes were walking around in Eastern Mostar as well. And I recognise, of course, that it's not easy from East Mostar to be able to say with a degree of certainty that you've heard everything that's exploding on Western Mostar or everything that's been shot out from Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's really what I was getting at. If someone can't hear a grenade hit because they're in an APC, how would that affect the numbers, the counting? The numbers, would it be in fact higher than what's -- what's been noted? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was telling you that not all of us were inside the vehicles. We had people outside the vehicles, and thus the counting cannot always be very precise in such a small place as East Mostar. But as I said, our patrol, at least we attempted to have patrols in Western Mostar, and they of course also note down what happens in that area and take a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were asked about the patrols in West Mostar, and again why weren't there patrols in West Mostar after dusk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all we didn't have a place for us to actually be, and conditions in West Mostar and the life there was easier than in East Mostar and thus did not really require permanent presence on our part until the moment when we had a base at which time then we actually had a detachment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Had you been present in East Mostar, however, during the night-time hours, you would be in a better position to know how many shells fell during those periods, as well as how many shells were sent out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer. I think you said East Mostar and we have East Mostar in the record, but did you mean East Mostar? Because the witness so far has said that he was in fact 24 hours present by the SpaBat in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No. I intended to say West Mostar. I was asking the witness about West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I, as I am talking anyway, may I ask two -- two different things. First is was it your own decision or were there some other reasons why you did not stay 24 hours in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The patrol schedule in Western Mostar was given to me by my task force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it was a SpaBat decision. It was not -- in other words, there was no indication of HVO authorities that would have prohibited you of staying in West Mostar as long as you liked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The other question --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I didn't get the interpretation in English of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you getting the English now? Is the English coming through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I cannot say with certainty whether the decision to remain in Western Mostar at night was a decision taken by my command or whether there were any objections or conditions that had been set out by HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other question is: To the extent that patrols were at the same time on both sides of the Neretva and noted impacts, was an effort made to correlate this? Were the impacts noted by the exact time so that one could see there is a mention from the east and it corresponds to an observation to the -- at the west and vice versa? Was that made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a recording of the impacts and the time at which they occurred, incoming or outgoing or when the actual explosion took place, but I do not recall actual cross-checking the data. The difference between incoming and outgoing fire, which is of course something that we saw mostly in Eastern Mostar, there was a large difference between the two, and that did not lead us to necessarily establish a correlation or a cause-and effect type of relation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, at one point in your cross-examination I thought you said and I wanted to ask you to affirm it or not, did you or others in your unit ever observe mortars or other weaponry positioned in the vicinity of the HVO hospital in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, and in some of the documents that are presented with my declaration I think there's mention of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The last document is, in that same binder, 5883. Witness, this is one of the Spanish Battalion reports that you referred to on your cross-examination, I believe by General Petkovic's attorney. And turning to page 3, item 6, this is a reference to the shelling incident that occurred on the day when there was a meeting at the -- I believe it was the city hall in East Mostar, between Spanish Battalion and the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that this answer reveals a confusion that I thought existed. In line 12 to my learned friend's question, whether they noticed the heavy weaponry near the HVO hospital in the west hospital, I don't think that the witness answered correctly. I believe that he meant East Mostar. In addition to that, during the cross-examination nobody ever asked any questions about the hospital in west hospital -- west -- in West Mostar. No arms were mentioned there. Can this be clarified before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked the witness -- I thought I heard him say during cross-examination that there were mortars or weaponry located in the vicinity -- observed in the vicinity of the HVO hospital in West Mostar, and that was the intent of my question. It's something that was said in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you may be right, but I do not remember that. Well, put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, the question is simply this, whether you recall you or others in your unit observed mortars or other weapons, artillery-type weapons, positioned in the area of the HVO hospital in West Mostar. And I'm asking it based on something the witness said during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, in the cross-examination there was no mention of the hospital in the West Mostar. If it is in the transcript, that is a mistake. Secondly and most importantly, if the Prosecution wants to put that question, could they please lay a foundation first of all. First he has to ask him whether he knew that there was an HVO hospital in West Mostar since the witness did not mention it anywhere, not during his testimony here and not in his statements. There is not a single word about this hospital anywhere. First we have to establish that he knows of the existence of this hospital, and then the question can be allowed. However, I keep my original objection that this question was not put in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On what line of the transcript did the witness mention this, i.e., that there were weapons close to the hospital in Mostar west?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're looking for it now. I believe it was during the cross-examination by General Praljak. What I propose is this: While our case manager is looking for the reference in the transcript to that, I'll move to that last document, ask about something else, and if we're able to find that reference I'll come back to it, and if I'm mistaken, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So, Witness, let's skip that one for the moment and go back then to this paragraph 6 of Exhibit 5883, P 05883. There's a reference here to successive corrections. It says with successive corrections made on target. And as a result of the attack, one lieutenant and a corporal were shrapnel injured at city hall entrance. Can you tell me what that means, successive corrections? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that if six mortar shells landed, the angle, the shooting angle, was corrected successively in order to hit the objective intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you just indicate for us briefly how does one go about correcting the shooting angle or what does that tell us about the intended objective or target in this instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really think that this question goes too far. One thing is what is stated in the report, and that is the first part of the question. I do not object to that. However, now the witness is again being asked as a witness, and the objection was raised vis-a-vis, asked that we shouldn't do that, how the procedure went. Then that means that the Defence will necessarily have to put a question, and at this stage we cannot put any further questions. So this is opening a new precise area in artillery science.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you know that as part of redirect after your redirect Defence counsel cannot put questions again afterwards, so the question has to be tied in to an answer he provided during cross-examination. If I remember correctly, during the cross-examination I don't think, with the exception of General Petkovic who mentioned where the mortars were positioned and the curves, but firing corrections or targets was a topic that was never mentioned so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what was mentioned, Mr. President, was the comment which was that the shelling incident was provocated by some outgoing ABiH shells. Counsel for Mr. Petkovic took the witness directly to this paragraph and asked specifically about this incident. And I think that if in fact a continual amount of shelling is taking place in which the position is repeatedly being corrected, it tends to shed light on whether the target of this shelling attack by the HVO was in fact Spanish Battalion or others who were in this -- in this location. So I think it's a fair question, and I'll accept your ruling on it however you decide, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. If we turn to paragraph 6, it is stated that the HVO fired shots because before that two ABiH mortars had fired shots. So this indicates that the HVO fired back. If you turn to the sentence that is immediately above, it seems that the HVO would have been engaged six mortars and would have adjusted the firing angle accordingly. But what is important, however, is that the origin of the fire is from the ABiH and not from the HVO. I don't think that this can be challenged because this is what is said here. Mr. Stringer, please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall saying -- you testified -- you were asked extensively about position of mortar weaponry in East Mostar. So the question is: In respect of this incident, do you recall seeing any outgoing mortar rounds in the vicinity of this specific incident at the city hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there at the time, but I recall that the officers who were going into the town hall building did hear the outgoing mortar rounds of the Armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again what would be meant by this use of "successive corrections made on target"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reported by the people by the people who were at the place where the grenades landed. I interpreted two landed some 200 metres away and others at 100 metres distance, and another one where they were. This is by way of example. But what I'm saying is that the landing point for the grenades came closer and closer so that the last shot would land where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And my last question is whether members of the Spanish Battalion when they met with officials of the HVO or with officials of the ABiH, whether then it was fair game for the other party to attack officials of the other side even when they were meeting with the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this question. It is not related at all to the cross-examination. If it pertains to the question from this document, it is obvious that the HVO reacted to provocations of BH army mortars. There was no mention at all of any meetings or the participants in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, what you want to know from the witness, Mr. Stringer, that is as follows: If after such an incident the ABiH fires and the HVO fires back. After a meeting together with the -- with UNPROFOR, is there a response from one or other party? Is that what you would like the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm sure I'm asking all of this poorly. I'm interested in this -- this successive corrections and what, if anything, that tells us about the intention of the people who were firing these mortar rounds, and successively correcting in a way that ultimately results in the wounding of Spanish Battalion personnel. So that's what I'm interested in asking the witness to address, if he can say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. The Prosecutor is now trying through this witness to get an answer to the effect that the HVO wanted to target the Spanish Battalion. If the Spanish Battalion thought that that was the case, they would have put it in their own report. So I think that this kind of question is malicious to say the least and unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, when they say successive corrections that result in the wounding of Spanish Battalion personnel, I think it is in the report, and that's what I'm asking you about. I think they did say it in the report, but I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor -- well, it's his document. He had this information before we started questioning the witness. If he's interested in that, then he should have asked about it in the direct examination. Again, I say that the question related to successive correction is a purely technical question, first and foremost for an expert. Here we heard from the representative of the government of Spain that they would rather not have the Court use witness as an expert. We're going back to the first thesis. The Prosecutor knew that full well, so he could have used the witness as an expert or the Prosecutor can call another expert witness. Your Honours, it is perfectly clear to you that this topic, after all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Witness, an incident occurred on that day. During that incident members of the SpaBat were injured. This is written down here, and you confirmed that. After that, was there a meeting between all the parties at the Spanish Battalion, the HVO, and the ABiH? Was there such a meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At this meeting were you present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was what was said at the meeting reported to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose I was briefed or told that the meeting was about to take place and that I was told something about it later, but I do not recall what subjects were broached at the meeting. The meeting took place before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting took place before what, before the shots were fired or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a meeting before the shelling, on the 4th Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Before. What I'm interested in is what happened afterwards? After your soldiers were injured, was there a meeting after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that incident possibly, but I cannot say with any certainty, but any sort of incident was in fact informed about to the implicated parties, the concerned parties particularly, when the concerned party in this case was the commander-in-chief of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you wanted to put a question to the witness when he can't tell us if there was a meeting after that, and you wanted to know what the conduct of one or other party was. But can't answer because he can't confirm that there was a meeting afterwards and he did not attend the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that, Mr. President, withdraw the question, and just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last point I'd like to address because we need to adjourn. What about this issue concerning the hospital in Mostar west? Have you found the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. We're going to withdraw that question as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the hearing is about to be adjourned. I would like to thank my colleagues, colleagues who cannot attend the latter part of the hearing. We will, of course, advise them of what has happened during the last part of the hearing thanks to the transcripts. I would like to thank the representative of the Spanish government for his contribution to this hearing. Before giving the floor to Defence counsel, I would like the usher to lower the blinds so that you can both leave the courtroom, and I wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now give the floor to the Defence counsel who wanted to say something. We are in open session. We will have to wait for the usher to come back into the courtroom for the blinds to be lifted, but we don't need to wait for the blinds to be lifted to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful, Your Honour. I have broached the subject to my learned friend for the Prosecution before the break. Your Honour, it is a matter that can be dealt with in open session, notwithstanding the fact that the focus of my submissions relate to a Prosecution filing which was confidential. But, Your Honour, the proceedings on this matter can be in open session. Your Honour, as you are aware, on the 28th of September the Prosecution replied to a joint Defence response relating to a Rule 71 bis application. In fact, it's Rule 81 bis application. Your Honour, that should have been the end of the matter as it was a reply, but rather adroitly the Prosecution managed to squeeze into that reply what amounts in effect to a fresh application. It was an application for Your Honours to consider by way of ex parte filing two documents. Now, Your Honour, it's a very simple matter, and it's my position it can be dealt with in way of five minutes of submission instead of having to bother Your Honours and my learned friends with paper filings and responses. Your Honours, I do know that the OTP reply by seeking to provide Your Honours with additional medical information effectively concedes that the initial application, the initial motion of the Prosecution, was deficient and deficient in a very material respect as contended by the Defence in its joint response. Your Honour, I also note that the OTP motion effectively acknowledges at least some merit in the Defence submissions regarding the proposed location for any videolink evidence that takes place, but, Your Honour, I must focus on the new information, which is the medical evidence that is hopefully to be placed before Your Honours. There is no objection on behalf of Mr. Bruno Stojic, and I understand I speak on behalf of my learned friends for the other accused, for that -- for those statements to go before the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, this witness, of course, is your witness, and the position of the Defence in the joint response was that Your Honours and the Defence were not privy to enough information in order to make an informed decision on what is a very important issue. But, Your Honour, it is completely untenable, in my respectful submission, for the Defence to pray in paragraph 3 of their reply, and Your Honour you might not have the reply with you but later on perhaps your assistants can print out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. Khan. We have been fully informed because we deliberated on the matter yesterday. So we are -- we know what it is about, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, but it's completely untenable in my submission for the Prosecution at paragraph 3 of their reply to say on the one hand, and I quote: "The witness is reluctant to share the details of her condition with the Trial Chamber and the parties," and yet in paragraph 4 to say Janus-faced, as it were, that the witness has provided two documents that provide additional information that explains the nature of her illness. And the impact on her ability to travel. So we are left with the singularly unsatisfactory position where the OTP, a party, no doubt they would accept, has the information, the organisation that the witness comes from has the information, the proposed legal advisor of that organisation has the information, and the Trial Chamber will very properly have that information. It is completely -- will have that information if the Prosecution's submission is granted. But it's completely inappropriate, in my submission, for the Defence to be left out in the cold. Your Honour, the Defence of course are not voyeurs, not withstanding that we do have one arsenal football team supporter, but we don't need the full medical records of this witness. But the general parameters of her condition, whether or not it's psychological or physiological, or whether it impacts on her ability to travel is necessary in my respectful submission. Your Honour, my learned friends in their reply say at paragraph 3 rather sharply, and they criticise the Defence for what is contended to be a cynical argument, that the witness was able to travel from her place of work to her home country for a diagnosis and treatment. But Your Honour that is half the story. That is not simply the focus of the complaint. What is extremely relevant is after going from her place of work to her home country, she was well enough to go back to work. So she is a witness that's able -- that's fit to go to work back after seeing the doctor, to travel internationally, and yet is not able to come to court. That calls, in my respectful submission, it calls and it necessitates an explanation and the burden is upon the Prosecution to show that the condition, the contended condition of this witness is so -- is sufficiently serious that it would be either wholly inappropriate or excessively burdensome for her to attend court rather than merely inconvenient. Your Honour, I say all of this, and being ignorant of the facts of this case because I've just joined this, but it may very well be the case that this witness knows she is in for some very robust cross-examination by my learned friends and the Defence teams, and the Defence of course and the accused in the dock will want to be satisfied that the accused is not seeking to hide behind a camera and not come before this court and being tested directly in the crucible of this court. Your Honour, if the condition of course is sufficiently serious, the Defence are not unreasonable one would hope, and it would be for the Defence to withdraw any objection if she does have a very legitimate reason. So Your Honour for all of those reasons I -- I do ask that at least the details as to the nature of the illness and the treatment be disclosed to the Defence. There is no objection at all for the Trial Chamber to have access to this information, but I do make one further remark. Of course the witness was called by the Prosecution. I did see His Honour Judge Trechsel shaking his head. Of course the witness was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The a witness was called by the Prosecution, but once the witness has given evidence-in-chief, he is a Court witness, your witness, Your Honour. And in my submission it's not the best practice, let me put it like that, it's not the best practice for a court witness to be contacting directly or indirectly at the Prosecution. The better practice in my respectful submission would have been for the legal advisor of the organisation concerned to have made an approach to the Victim and Witnesses Unit, and Your Honours could make the decision but Your Honours those are my hopefully brief submissions on this issue I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move back into closed session, please, registrar.
